analysis.one_liner: Requires federal contractors to pay workers a living wage of at least $7.50 an hour.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it was referred to two House committees in May 1996 and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: Any company with a federal contract or subcontract worth more than $10,000 would have to pay every worker on that contract at least $7.50 an hour, or enough for a full-time worker to lift a family of four above the federal poverty line — whichever is higher. Companies that failed to pay would lose their federal contracts for five years and owe workers their back wages plus an equal amount in damages. Small businesses and nonprofits whose CEO pay is modest (25-to-1 or less) would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers employed on federal contracts — janitors, food service workers, construction and service workers on government jobs — would see their pay rise to a living-wage floor. Taxpayers would also benefit indirectly: contractors underpaying workers on government-funded jobs would have to pay back wages plus equal damages if caught.

how_it_helps.text: Employers on federal contracts of $10,000 or more must pay each worker on the contract the greater of $7.50 an hour or an hourly wage that, at 40 hours a week, reaches the federal poverty level for a family of four.

Contractors who fail to pay the living wage face contract suspension, a five-year ban on new federal contracts, and liability for unpaid wages plus an equal amount in liquidated damages, which the Labor Secretary would pay to the affected workers.
The bill blocks employers from sidestepping the wage floor by laying off workers and replacing them with trainees who are exempt from the requirement.
The bill's findings note that federal contractors benefit from billions of dollars a year in federal spending and tax subsidies, arguing public dollars should not fund poverty wages.

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors with low-wage workforces would bear the cost of higher wages, and those costs could flow into higher bids on government work — meaning taxpayers could pay somewhat more for some federal contracts. Nonprofits with CEO-to-worker pay ratios above 25-to-1 would also lose their exemption from the requirement.

drawbacks.text: Higher contractor wages would likely raise the cost of federal procurement, so taxpayers could pay more for some government services and goods.

The bill carves out broad exemptions: all small businesses, most nonprofits, and employees in apprenticeship or training programs up to six months are excluded, narrowing how many workers the floor actually covers.

A $7.50 federal floor was more than double the 1996 federal minimum wage of $4.75, a jump that critics would argue could reduce competition among contractors and push some small subcontractors out of the market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers directly covered, the benefit is substantial: a guaranteed wage that could roughly double the pay of some federal contract workers, backed by real enforcement (contract loss and double damages). The main cost is procurement — some federal contracts would cost taxpayers more — and the design blunts that with exemptions for small businesses and modest-pay nonprofits. The bill is narrow (only contract workers, not all workers), but within its scope it is a direct, enforceable wage floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, which sent it to subcommittees where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the Federal Living Wage Responsibility Act on May 15, 1996, with 22 cosponsors (21 Democrats and 1 Independent).
The House referred the bill to the Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee and the Government Reform and Oversight Committee on the day it was introduced.

Within a week, the bill was sent to subcommittees — the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology on May 21 and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on June 7 — and never advanced further.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors with low-wage workforces are better off because the bill died — they never had to raise pay to $7.50 an hour or face debarment. Low-wage contract workers are worse off; the wage floor never took effect, and the House GOP majority's committees that buried it faced no recorded vote on the merits.

for.name: Rep. Luis Gutierrez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to set a living-wage floor for federal contract workers.

for.name: 22 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors (21 Democrats, 1 Independent); none was a Republican.

against.name: House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup; referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it sat.

against.name: House Government Reform and Oversight Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology; no action followed.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and the bill sat in the committees of a House controlled by Republicans with no recorded votes, so the fight never produced a public tally.

industries.industry: Federal contractors with low-wage workforces (janitorial, food service, light construction, call-center and clerical services)
industries.note: The bill would force them to raise pay for contract workers to at least $7.50 an hour and repay stolen wages with double damages. Their interest in stopping it ran directly against the contract workers it covered.
Small business concerns are fully exempt from the wage floor, so they avoid the compliance cost that larger contractors would bear.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt nonprofits with high CEO pay
industries.note: Nonprofits are exempt only if their CEO makes no more than 25 times the pay of their lowest-paid full-time-equivalent worker; nonprofits above that ratio would have to comply, while most modest-pay charities would not.
